clinicalPearls: The commonest congenital sideroblastic anaemia, caused by mutations in ALAS2, the erythroid-specific delta-aminolaevulinate synthase catalysing the first, pyridoxine-dependent step of haem synthesis
X-linked, so it classically affects males; carrier females are usually mild or unaffected but can be symptomatic through skewed lyonisation, sometimes presenting only in later life
Produces a microcytic, hypochromic anaemia with a characteristic dimorphic blood film and ring sideroblasts (iron-laden mitochondria encircling the erythroblast nucleus) on marrow iron staining
Many cases are pyridoxine (vitamin B6) responsive because the enzyme uses pyridoxal phosphate as a cofactor, so a therapeutic trial is warranted
Systemic iron overload is characteristic and occurs independently of transfusion, driven by ineffective erythropoiesis and hepcidin suppression, and may be the dominant clinical problem
In contrast with iron deficiency, the anaemia is microcytic but iron stores are high, so iron supplementation is harmful
Co-inheritance of an HFE haemochromatosis variant can accentuate iron loading, and the X-linked pattern with a supportive family history aids diagnosis
reference.pathophysiology: X-linked sideroblastic anaemia results from loss-of-function or hypomorphic mutations in ALAS2 on the X chromosome, encoding the erythroid isoform of delta-aminolaevulinate synthase, which condenses glycine and succinyl-CoA using pyridoxal 5'-phosphate as cofactor in the first and rate-limiting step of haem biosynthesis. Deficient enzyme activity leaves iron that has entered the erythroblast mitochondrion unincorporated into protoporphyrin, so iron accumulates within perinuclear mitochondria to form ring sideroblasts. The impaired haemoglobinisation produces a microcytic hypochromic anaemia with ineffective erythropoiesis, while suppressed hepcidin drives increased dietary iron absorption and progressive systemic iron overload.
additionalDifferentials: Other congenital sideroblastic anaemias (SLC25A38 and mitochondrial or syndromic forms)
Acquired sideroblastic anaemia or myelodysplasia with ring sideroblasts
Thalassaemia trait and other microcytic anaemias
Lead poisoning and copper deficiency or zinc excess
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film, showing a dimorphic hypochromic microcytic population
Bone marrow aspirate with Perls (Prussian blue) stain for ring sideroblasts
Iron studies with ferritin and transferrin saturation (raised), to distinguish from iron deficiency
ALAS2 gene sequencing, with a broader sideroblastic anaemia panel if negative
A trial of pyridoxine to assess responsiveness
Hepatic and cardiac iron quantification by MRI (T2*)
HFE genotyping where iron overload is prominent
redFlags: Iron overload with cardiac, hepatic or endocrine dysfunction
Inappropriate iron therapy worsening iron loading
Family history of unexplained iron overload or anaemia in males
reference.prognosis: Pyridoxine-responsive disease often has a good outlook with correction or improvement of the anaemia, but iron overload remains the principal threat and requires lifelong monitoring. Non-responsive or transfusion-dependent cases carry greater morbidity, much of it preventable with chelation and, where appropriate, venesection.
pitfalls: Treating the microcytic anaemia as iron deficiency and giving iron, which aggravates overload
Overlooking symptomatic female carriers because the condition is labelled X-linked
Missing iron overload because the patient has never been transfused
Attributing ring sideroblasts to myelodysplasia without considering a congenital cause in a younger patient
management: A therapeutic trial of pyridoxine, to which many cases respond given the enzyme's pyridoxal-phosphate cofactor dependence
Strict avoidance of iron supplementation, which is harmful because iron stores are already high
Iron chelation therapy for established systemic iron overload
Red cell transfusion support for pyridoxine-unresponsive or severe anaemia
Monitoring of iron burden with ferritin, transferrin saturation and hepatic and cardiac MRI
Haematology follow-up including assessment of carrier females, who may become symptomatic in later life
Genetic counselling with ALAS2 testing for the family
